newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Woolwich to return cash, invest.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Woolwich to return cash, invest.

text.p: British building society-turned-bank Woolwich will return cash to shareholders at the same time as investing to improve returns to them, its chief executive said on Monday.

"We believe in using our capital carefully, but also in giving some of it back and doing those two things simultaneously," John Stewart told Reuters after the Woolwich shares made a higher-than-expected debut on the London stock exchange.
Woolwich shares opened at 368 pence on their debut, but had slipped back to 339.5 pence by 1105 GMT.
Stewart said a combination of a buoyant market, a strong banking sector and the fact Woolwich was "a very attractive set of businesses" were behind what he admitted was a greater-than-expected price.

Analysts had expected the Woolwich, which shed a 150-year mutual tradition to convert to a bank and float on the stock exchange, to debut at around 320 pence. This was substantially higher than its own initial estimates of 175-200 pence in January.
Stewart said Woolwich already had "a great group of businesses" with all the elements in terms of diversification it needed.
And he was confident Woolwich could perform well in a whole range of personal financial services and justify the market's expectations of it.
Woolwich was making headway at reducing its cost base, but this would involve technological improvements rather than job losses or branch closures, Stewart said.
"We are working smarter, not working harder."

Stewart said Woolwich was taking great care in looking at ways of returning cash to shareholders but could not give a timetable for when this might be or any indication of how much the return would total.
But it would probably take proposals on the issue to shareholders early next year.
He admitted the bank had "an incredibly high" tier one capital ratio of around 13 percent. Analysts said this could be brought down to 7.0 to 7.5 percent.
"We estimate that the Woolwich has about 750 million pounds of tier one equity capital beyond its immediate needs," Salomon Brothers analyst John Leonard said in a recent research paper on Woolwich.
Woolwich would weigh up whether it was worth losing a protected status against hostile takeovers by making acquisitions itself by assessing if such a move was in shareholders' interests.
But Stewart did not rule out a merger or agreeing to a takeover if the bank was approached by another party.
So far no such approach had been made, he added.
